At 4:17 every afternoon, the town lost one minute.

Nobody noticed at first. Clocks continued to tick, trains arrived when expected, and dinner burned at the usual rate. But small things began to go missing from memory. A woman would stand in her kitchen with a knife in her hand and wonder whether she had already chopped the onions. A boy would open his schoolbook and find a sentence underlined in his own handwriting, though he could not remember reading it.

Then the clocks began to disagree.

The clock in the bakery showed 4:16. The clock in the church tower showed 4:18. The clock above the pharmacy door, which had been broken since winter, showed 4:17 exactly and never moved again.

People complained for a week, then adapted. Humans are good at adapting to the inexplicable. They put notes on their wrists. They tied ribbons around doorknobs. They began saying, “If I forget, remind me,” though they could not say what it was they feared forgetting.

Only Mara kept watch.

She lived above the old railway station in two rooms that shook whenever a freight train passed, though no freight trains had passed through the town in twenty-three years. Her father had been the stationmaster, and after he died she inherited the building, the brass key cabinet, and a habit of listening for arrivals.

Every afternoon, at 4:16, Mara climbed the tower stairs.

At the top was a window facing east. From there she could see the whole town: the bakery chimney breathing flour into the sky, the river curling behind the houses, the schoolyard with its rusted swings. She carried a notebook and wrote down everything she could remember.

At 4:16, the sun touched the roof of the courthouse.

At 4:17, the bells in the church gave a single, muffled note.

At 4:18, there was always a sound like paper tearing.

She had heard it for twelve days.

On the thirteenth, someone knocked on the station door.

Mara found a girl standing outside in a yellow coat. She looked about ten years old and held a red balloon by its string. The balloon floated beside her shoulder, trembling in the wind.

“Are you Mara?” the girl asked.

“Yes.”

“I’m supposed to give you this.”

She held out a small envelope.

There was no name on it. Inside, Mara found a photograph of the railway station as it had been long ago, when the platform was crowded and the tracks shone like black ribbons. In the picture, her father stood beside a younger version of himself. He was smiling.

On the back, someone had written:

*The minute is not lost. It is being kept.*

Mara looked at the girl. “Who gave you this?”

“My mother.”

“Where is your mother?”

The girl pointed toward the tracks.

There were no tracks there. Not anymore. Only weeds, gravel, and the shallow trench where the rails had been removed.

The girl’s red balloon slipped from her hand.

It rose silently, caught by a wind that seemed to come from underground.

Mara ran.

She followed it past the platform, past the weeds, to the old tunnel mouth beyond the river. The tunnel had been sealed with bricks for as long as she could remember, but now a narrow opening stood in the center, black and breathing cold air.

From within came the sound of a train.

Mara stepped through.

The tunnel opened into a station that did not belong to any map. Lamps glowed along the platform. A timetable hung from the ceiling, its letters rearranging themselves every few seconds. People waited on benches: a man holding a dead bouquet, a woman with a suitcase, three children in matching coats. They were all staring at their hands as if trying to remember why they had come.

At the far end stood a train made of dark wood and silver windows.

The girl’s mother was there.

She was young—too young, Mara thought—and wore a blue scarf. When she saw her daughter, she smiled with relief.

“You found her,” Mara said.

“No,” the woman replied. “She found me.”

The train gave a low whistle.

“What is this place?” Mara asked.

“The minute,” said the woman. “Every day, one minute slips out of the world. It comes here. People can enter if they have something unfinished.”

“Why would anyone want to stay?”

The woman looked down at her daughter. “Because unfinished things are warm.”

Mara understood then. The minute was filled with everything people had almost said, almost done, almost forgiven. It held the hand not taken, the letter never sent, the apology swallowed at the dinner table. It was a room beneath time where abandoned possibilities continued breathing.

“Your father came here,” the woman said.

Mara felt the station tilt beneath her feet.

“He came every day after your mother died. He wanted one more minute with her. He kept returning until the door closed behind him.”

Mara remembered her father’s final morning: his coat on the chair, his coffee untouched, the brass key missing from its hook. She had been eight years old. She had thought he had left because he was tired of being sad.

“Can I see him?”

The woman nodded toward the train.

Mara climbed aboard.

Inside, the air smelled of dust and rain. She passed through one carriage, then another. In each window she saw a different moment: a wedding, a hospital room, a child asleep in a car, snow falling on a town that had not yet been built.

In the last carriage, her father sat alone.

He looked exactly as he had in the photograph, except for the silver in his hair. He held the brass station key between both hands.

“Mara,” he said.

She wanted to run to him. She wanted to strike him. She wanted to become eight years old again and climb into his lap.

Instead she stood in the doorway.

“You left.”

“I know.”

“You could have come back.”

“I tried.”

“No, you didn’t.”

He lowered his eyes. “You’re right.”

The honesty of it hurt more than any excuse.

Outside, the train began to move.

“You have to go,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because the minute is closing. You cannot live in what almost happened.”

Mara sat beside him. For a while neither spoke.

Then she placed the brass key in his palm.

“I remember you,” she said. “That has to be enough.”

Her father closed his fingers around the key. “It is.”

The train slowed. The door opened onto the dark tunnel.

Mara stepped down.

Behind her, the train began to fade—not vanish, exactly, but become less certain, like a thought losing its edges. Her father raised one hand.

At 4:18, the sound of paper tearing filled the tunnel.

Then everything was quiet.

Mara emerged beside the river at dusk. The girl in the yellow coat was waiting there. Her mother stood beside her, crying and laughing at once.

That evening, for the first time in thirteen days, every clock in town agreed.

At 4:17, the church bell rang.

At 4:18, it rang again.

And in the station tower, Mara opened her notebook to a blank page and wrote:

*Today, nothing was lost.*

Then she went downstairs to make tea, leaving the door unlocked in case someone else came looking for what they had almost forgotten.
